title: Drying, Curing and Storage Quality Control

content.overview: Harvest does not stop plant-material change. Drying moves water from internal tissues toward the surface and then into surrounding air; curing/conditioning allows moisture to redistribute under controlled storage; packaging changes exposure to water vapor, oxygen, light and physical damage; and storage temperature/time influence stability. Postharvest quality therefore depends on measured process conditions rather than touch, calendar days or room setpoints alone.

vocabulary.definition: The controlled removal of water from harvested plant material after harvest.
A controlled post-drying holding period used to stabilize moisture distribution and product characteristics.
A measure related to how available water is for chemical reactions and microbial growth in a material.
The ability of harvested material to maintain quality and chemical characteristics over time under defined conditions.

sections.title: Drying is a controlled moisture-removal process
sections.body: Drying should remove water at a controlled rate rather than as quickly as possible. Temperature, relative humidity, airflow, flower density, and load size influence how moisture moves from internal tissues to the surrounding air.

sections.title: Curing follows initial drying
sections.body: After initial drying, moisture can continue to redistribute within harvested material. Curing uses managed storage conditions to allow equilibration while monitoring for excessive moisture, degradation, or contamination risk.

sections.title: Packaging creates a storage environment
sections.body: Packaging influences exposure to moisture, oxygen, light, and physical damage. The package should therefore be considered part of the storage system rather than a neutral container added after quality decisions are finished.

sections.title: Storage conditions affect stability
sections.body: Temperature, light, oxygen, and time can influence the stability of harvested cannabis constituents. Consistent storage conditions and documented handling are important when comparing quality changes over time.

workedExamples: Flower exteriors feel dry while denser interiors remain wetter. Surface feel alone cannot establish uniform moisture status; continue representative measurement and controlled conditioning.
Two drying zones share the same thermostat/RH setpoints, but one has much higher local airflow. Drying rate and uniformity can differ even when room averages match.
A batch reaches its intended dry endpoint but is packaged while moisture distribution is still uneven. Later equilibration can create localized high-moisture conditions inside the package.
Material stored warm and exposed to light changes faster than material protected from heat/light. Storage remains an active quality-control phase.
commonMistakes: Using touch alone to determine drying endpoint.
Assuming room setpoints equal actual product microclimate.
Maximizing airflow without checking uneven or excessively rapid drying.
Packaging before moisture is sufficiently stable/uniform.
Ignoring temperature, oxygen and light after packaging.
content.practicalApplication: Create a batch drying record with representative room and product observations across multiple locations and times. Track temperature, RH, airflow context, product moisture/weight or other approved endpoint metric, and spatial differences. Continue through packaging/conditioning and document whether moisture remains stable after equilibration.
content.summary: Post-harvest quality depends on controlled moisture removal, stabilization, packaging, and storage. Drying and curing are active process-control stages, and the storage environment continues to influence harvested material after those stages are complete.

blocks.title: Drying is mass transfer
blocks.body: Water moves from wetter internal tissues toward the material surface and then into the surrounding air. Temperature, RH, airflow, flower size/density and load arrangement all influence the rate and uniformity of that process.

blocks.title: Postharvest process variables
rows: Representative RH, not one distant sensor
Approved measurement method and representative sample

items.title: Identify the batch
items.body: Preserve lot identity and harvest time/context.

items.title: Map the drying environment
items.body: Measure representative temperature/RH and note airflow/load geometry.

items.title: Track product change
items.body: Use the approved weight/moisture/water-activity or other process method consistently.

items.title: Check spatial uniformity
items.body: Compare representative locations instead of one convenient sample.

items.title: Condition/equilibrate
items.body: Allow moisture distribution to stabilize under controlled conditions.

items.title: Package and verify
items.body: Confirm the package/storage environment does not reintroduce instability.

items.title: Trend deviations
items.body: Use batch records to identify repeatable hot spots, slow zones or handling problems.

blocks.title: Dry outside, wet inside
blocks.setting: Dense flowers feel dry at the surface, but representative internal measurements remain higher and variable.
options: Package immediately because the surface feels dry
Continue controlled drying/conditioning and representative measurement
Increase heat aggressively until every surface is brittle
blocks.answer: Continue controlled drying/conditioning and representative measurement.
blocks.feedback: Surface feel can lead product-average moisture status and does not prove uniformity.

blocks.title: Interpret a drying-room trend
blocks.instructions: Review time-series environmental and product data from three drying zones.
prompts: Identify the fastest and slowest drying zones.
Flag any location that may be over- or under-drying.
Decide what additional product measurement is needed before packaging.
Describe how you would verify stability after conditioning.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Postharvest is a measured process from harvest through storage. Room setpoints and surface feel are not substitutes for representative product and environmental evidence.

primaryVisuals.title: Room conditions do not equal product state
primaryVisuals.alt: Drying-process diagram separating room temperature and relative humidity from representative product measurements such as moisture content and water activity, with rack position, loading, airflow and time included so spatial and temporal differences can be evaluated without substituting one measurement for another.
primaryVisuals.caption: Room RH is not product water activity, and moisture content and water activity are not interchangeable. Combine room history with representative product measurements by position and time.
